nameStory: Salad burnet gets its name from its culinary use - the leaves taste like cucumber with a hint of watermelon and were traditionally tossed into salads for flavor. The word 'burnet' comes from the French 'brunette,' referring to the brownish color of the dried plant, while the genus name Sanguisorba means 'blood-absorber' because it was once used to stop bleeding.
description: Salad burnet is a small perennial herb that looks like a delicate, ferny plant with unusual crimson pom-pom flowers. It typically grows 10-22 inches tall (though it can be much shorter in dry conditions) with deeply toothed, compound leaves that give it an almost fern-like appearance. The most distinctive feature is its spherical, dark red flower clusters that sit atop thin stems well above the foliage. This drought-tolerant plant has a massive taproot that can extend up to 3 feet deep, allowing it to survive in challenging conditions.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Distinctive crimson or dark red spherical flower heads about the size of a marble, sitting on thin stems that rise well above the leaves - they look like tiny burgundy pom-poms

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Compound leaves with deeply toothed, oval leaflets arranged along a central stem, giving the plant a delicate, ferny appearance - crush a leaf and smell the fresh cucumber-like fragrance

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Low-growing rosette of leaves with flower stems rising above - stays green most of the year even in cold climates, forming neat clumps

idTips.label: Taste Test
idTips.description: Young leaves have a distinctive cucumber-watermelon flavor when chewed - this edible plant was historically used in salads and beverages

habitat: Salad burnet thrives in dry, well-drained soils and can often be found in rocky areas, old fields, and disturbed sites where other plants struggle. It prefers sunny locations and alkaline soils, making it common along roadsides and in abandoned lots. With only 4 recorded observations in New England, it's quite rare in our region and most likely to be found as an escape from cultivation near old homesteads or herb gardens.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges early and the ferny foliage becomes more prominent. The distinctive compound leaves are fresh and bright green, perfect for taste-testing the cucumber flavor.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming time when the characteristic crimson pom-pom flowers appear on tall, thin stems above the foliage. This is when the plant is most easily identified from a distance.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade but the evergreen to semi-evergreen foliage remains green and identifiable. Seeds develop and the plant may begin to look slightly less vibrant.
seasonality.winter: In New England, the leaves typically stay green until heavy snow cover, making it one of the few herbs that remain somewhat identifiable through much of winter.

funFact: Salad burnet was so valued by medieval drinkers that it earned the nickname 'Toper's plant' because it was added to wine and ale - people believed it prevented intoxication and hangovers, though it was probably just the refreshing cucumber taste that made drinks more palatable!
confusionNotes: The ferny foliage might be confused with other compound-leaved plants, but no other plant in New England has those distinctive dark red spherical flower heads on thin stems. If you're not seeing the crimson pom-pom flowers, crush a leaf - that cucumber smell is a dead giveaway.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'salad burnet,' this plant is quite rare in New England and you're much more likely to encounter it in herb gardens or as a garden escape than in truly wild settings. Many field guides focus on more common species, so finding this one in the wild would be a real botanical treasure hunt.
compareHints: Unlike its relatives Canadian burnet and great burnet which are native and have white or pink flowers, salad burnet has those distinctive dark crimson flower heads and is much smaller overall. Great burnet can grow over 3 feet tall with elongated flower spikes, while Canadian burnet has white bottlebrush-like flowers - salad burnet's red pom-poms are unmistakable among the burnets.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Canadian burnet is the tallest burnet species you'll find in New England, easily distinguished from its relatives by its creamy white flowers (great burnet has dark red flowers, while salad burnet has tiny greenish flowers with red tips).
Great burnet towers over its relatives, reaching 3-6 feet compared to Canadian burnet's 2-4 feet and salad burnet's modest 1-2 feet.
Siberian Burnet is the only burnet in New England with drooping flower spikes - all other burnets have upright flower heads.
